title: Java Syntax
learningObjectives: Identify the class declaration and main method in a simple Java program.
Explain the role of braces in defining code blocks.
Recognize statements and the use of semicolons.
Distinguish case-sensitive identifiers and valid Java naming.
Read and write a short Java program with correct source structure.

understand.concept: Java syntax is the set of rules that determines how Java source code must be written. A simple beginner application is commonly placed in a class. The main method provides the entry point used by the Java launcher in this course. Braces group declarations and statements into blocks, and semicolons terminate many Java statements. Java identifiers are case-sensitive.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct syntax lets the compiler understand the program. Learning the structure early makes compiler messages easier to interpret and prevents errors as code grows.
understand.analogy: Braces are like boundaries around a section of a document: they show which statements belong together. Semicolons mark the end of many individual statements.
understand.analogyLimit: Java syntax has exceptions and special constructs. Not every declaration ends with a semicolon, and modern Java supports additional source-file forms beyond the classic class-and-main structure.

explain.narrative:
## A basic program structure

A beginner program often declares `public class Main`, then declares `public static void main(String[] args)` inside the class. Statements inside the method are enclosed by braces. The `System.out.println(...)` statement ends with a semicolon.

## Case sensitivity

Java distinguishes uppercase and lowercase letters. `Main`, `main` and `MAIN` are three different identifiers.

## Identifiers

Identifiers name classes, methods, variables and other declarations. They cannot be Java keywords and must follow Java's identifier rules. By convention, class names commonly use UpperCamelCase and method or variable names use lowerCamelCase.

## Whitespace and formatting

Spaces, line breaks and indentation help people read code. Java generally does not use indentation to define blocks; braces do that. Consistent formatting makes nested blocks and statement boundaries easier to inspect.

practise.guidedTask: Correct a sample program by checking that the public class is named Main, the main method is inside the class, braces are paired and the println statement ends with a semicolon.
practise.independentTask: Write a program with two integer variables named `firstValue` and `secondValue`, then print their sum. Change the case of one variable reference and observe the compiler diagnostic.
hints: Check opening and closing braces as pairs.
Check the spelling and capitalization of every identifier.
A method call used as a statement normally ends with a semicolon.
practise.challenge: Review your program against the expected behaviour, then explain one likely error and how you would diagnose it.

questions.prompt: Which symbol normally terminates a Java statement?
questions.explanation: Many Java statements end with a semicolon.
Java treats identifiers with different capitalization as different names.

questions.prompt: What do braces define in a basic Java class and method?
questions.explanation: Braces group class and method bodies and other blocks.

questions.prompt: Which is the conventional class name style?
questions.explanation: Java class names conventionally begin each word with an uppercase letter.

questions.prompt: Which pair represents two different identifiers in Java?
questions.explanation: Java is case-sensitive, so total and Total are different identifiers.
